name: Sore throat
summary: A sore throat is very common and is usually caused by a virus such as a cold or flu. It typically gets better on its own within a week.
redFlags: Difficulty breathing
Unable to swallow, or drooling because you cannot swallow saliva
A high-pitched noise when breathing in (stridor)
Severe symptoms that are getting worse quickly
Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat
urgentFlags: A very high temperature, or feeling hot and shivery
Signs of dehydration, such as peeing less or dark urine
A weakened immune system, for example from chemotherapy or uncontrolled diabetes
Severe pain on one side of the throat with difficulty opening the mouth or a muffled voice

commonCauses.title: Viral infections
commonCauses.detail: Colds, flu and COVID-19 are the most common causes; antibiotics do not help.

commonCauses.title: Tonsillitis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed tonsils, usually viral but sometimes bacterial, such as strep throat.

commonCauses.title: Glandular fever
commonCauses.detail: A viral infection causing a severe sore throat, swollen glands and tiredness, mostly in young people.

commonCauses.title: Irritation
commonCauses.detail: Smoking, dry air, acid reflux and shouting can make the throat sore.

selfCare: Gargle with warm salty water (adults only)
Drink plenty of fluids, and try cool or soft foods
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Suck ice cubes, ice lollies or lozenges (not for young children)
Rest, and ask a pharmacist whether you need further treatment
avoid: Expecting antibiotics for a viral sore throat
Smoking or smoky places
Very hot drinks that can scald the throat
seeDoctorIf: Your sore throat has not improved after a week
You often get sore throats
You have a sore throat with a lump in your mouth or neck
A child under 5 needs help for a sore throat

name: Hoarse voice or lost voice
summary: A hoarse or lost voice is often caused by laryngitis from a cold or from straining your voice. It usually gets better within 1 to 2 weeks.
redFlags: Difficulty breathing or a high-pitched noise when breathing in
Unable to swallow saliva or drooling
Hoarseness with sudden swelling of the throat, lips or tongue
urgentFlags: It is very painful or difficult to swallow
Coughing up blood with a hoarse voice
Sudden hoarseness after an injury to the neck

commonCauses.title: Laryngitis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed voice box, usually from a cold or flu virus.

commonCauses.title: Voice strain
commonCauses.detail: Shouting, singing or talking a lot can make the voice hoarse.

commonCauses.title: Acid reflux
commonCauses.detail: Stomach acid coming up the throat can irritate the voice box.

commonCauses.title: Smoking and irritants
commonCauses.detail: Smoke, dust and fumes can cause long-lasting hoarseness.

commonCauses.title: Growths on the vocal cords
commonCauses.detail: Nodules, polyps or, rarely, cancer can cause hoarseness that lasts for weeks.

selfCare: Rest your voice and speak as little as possible
Drink plenty of fluids
Keep the air moist, for example with bowls of water near radiators
Gargle with warm salty water (adults only)
avoid: Whispering or talking loudly, which both strain the voice
Smoking
Clearing your throat repeatedly
seeDoctorIf: Hoarseness has not improved after 2 weeks
You keep getting voice problems
You smoke and have a hoarse voice that is not going away

name: Difficulty swallowing
summary: Difficulty swallowing means food or drink is hard to get down or feels stuck. A short-lived problem with a sore throat is common, but ongoing swallowing difficulty should always be checked.
redFlags: Unable to swallow saliva, or drooling
Difficulty breathing, or noisy high-pitched breathing
Food stuck in the throat or chest that will not move and you cannot swallow anything
Sudden difficulty swallowing with face drooping, weakness or slurred speech
Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat
urgentFlags: Ongoing difficulty swallowing
Coughing or choking while eating or drinking
Feeling that food sticks in your throat or chest
Bringing food back up, or a wet, gurgly voice after eating
Losing weight without trying

commonCauses.title: Sore throat or tonsillitis
commonCauses.detail: Pain and swelling make swallowing uncomfortable for a few days.

commonCauses.title: Acid reflux
commonCauses.detail: Can inflame or narrow the food pipe.

commonCauses.title: Neurological conditions
commonCauses.detail: Stroke, Parkinson's disease and other conditions can affect the swallowing muscles.

commonCauses.title: Narrowing or growth in the food pipe
commonCauses.detail: Including, less commonly, cancer of the oesophagus.

selfCare: Sit upright to eat and drink, and stay upright for a while afterwards
Take small bites and chew well
Choose softer, moist foods while you are waiting to be seen
avoid: Eating while lying down or rushing meals
Ignoring swallowing problems that keep happening
seeDoctorIf: You keep having difficulty swallowing
You get frequent chest infections
You have heartburn or acid reflux most days

name: Swollen glands in the neck
summary: Swollen glands (lymph nodes) in the neck are usually a sign your body is fighting an infection such as a cold or sore throat. They normally go down within about 2 weeks.
redFlags: Swollen glands with difficulty breathing
Swollen neck with a very sore throat and inability to swallow saliva or drooling
A rapidly spreading red, hot swelling of the neck with fever
urgentFlags: Swollen glands and finding it very difficult to swallow
Swollen glands with a very high temperature and feeling very unwell

commonCauses.title: Colds and throat infections
commonCauses.detail: The most common reason glands swell; they shrink as the infection clears.

commonCauses.title: Ear, tooth or skin infections
commonCauses.detail: Infections near the neck often cause nearby glands to swell.

commonCauses.title: Glandular fever and other viruses
commonCauses.detail: Can cause swollen glands for several weeks.

commonCauses.title: Rarely, cancer
commonCauses.detail: Such as lymphoma or leukaemia, usually with hard, painless glands that keep growing.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if they are sore, following the pack instructions
Treat the underlying cold or sore throat
avoid: Squeezing or massaging a swollen gland
Ignoring a lump that keeps growing
seeDoctorIf: The glands are getting bigger or have not gone down after a week or two
They feel hard or do not move when you press them
You have night sweats or unexplained weight loss
You have no other signs of infection
The swelling is just above or below the collarbone

name: Feeling of a lump in the throat
summary: Many people feel like there is a lump or tightness in the throat even when nothing is there. It is often linked to stress, acid reflux or mucus, and is usually harmless, but real difficulty swallowing should be checked.
redFlags: Difficulty breathing or noisy breathing
Unable to swallow saliva
Sudden throat tightness with swelling of the lips, tongue or face, or a rash
urgentFlags: Food actually sticking or difficulty swallowing food or drink
Pain when swallowing
Losing weight without trying
A lump you can see or feel in the neck

commonCauses.title: Globus sensation
commonCauses.detail: A harmless feeling of a lump, often worse with stress and easier when eating.

commonCauses.title: Acid reflux
commonCauses.detail: Acid can irritate the throat and cause a tight feeling.

commonCauses.title: Catarrh or postnasal drip
commonCauses.detail: Mucus at the back of the throat makes you want to keep swallowing.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Tension in the throat muscles is common during anxiety.

selfCare: Sip water and swallow gently rather than repeatedly clearing your throat
Try relaxation or breathing exercises if stress makes it worse
Avoid eating late at night if you have reflux
avoid: Repeatedly clearing your throat or swallowing dry
Smoking
seeDoctorIf: The feeling lasts more than a few weeks
It is getting worse or is only on one side
You also have a hoarse voice or ear pain

name: Nose injury or broken nose
summary: A blow to the nose can cause pain, swelling, bruising and a nosebleed. Most nose injuries heal on their own within a few weeks.
redFlags: A nosebleed that will not stop
Clear, watery fluid trickling from the nose
A large cut, or something in the wound
Severe headache with blurred or double vision, or eye pain with double vision
Neck pain or stiffness with numbness or tingling in the arms
A purple swelling inside the nose
Vomiting, passing out or difficulty speaking
urgentFlags: The nose looks crooked after the injury
Swelling has not started to go down after 3 days
Painkillers are not helping
Still hard to breathe through the nose once swelling has gone
Regular nosebleeds or a high temperature after the injury

commonCauses.title: Bruised nose
commonCauses.detail: Pain and swelling without broken bone; settles within a week or two.

commonCauses.title: Broken nose
commonCauses.detail: Common after sports, falls or fights; may change the shape of the nose.

commonCauses.title: Septal haematoma
commonCauses.detail: A collection of blood inside the nose that needs urgent drainage.

selfCare: Hold an ice pack wrapped in a cloth on the nose for up to 20 minutes every few hours
Take paracetamol for pain, following the pack instructions
Keep your head raised, including when sleeping
Treat any nosebleed by leaning forward and pinching the soft part of the nose
avoid: Trying to straighten your nose yourself
Picking or blowing your nose until it has healed
Contact sports for at least 6 weeks
seeDoctorIf: Your nose looks a different shape once swelling has gone
You have ongoing breathing problems through your nose

name: Catarrh or mucus in the throat
summary: Catarrh is a build-up of mucus in the nose, sinuses and back of the throat. It usually follows a cold or comes with allergies and clears up on its own.
redFlags: Difficulty breathing
Swelling around the eyes with fever or vision changes
urgentFlags: Feeling very unwell with a high temperature
Blood-stained mucus from one side of the nose

commonCauses.title: Colds and sinusitis
commonCauses.detail: Infections make the lining of the nose produce more mucus.

commonCauses.title: Allergies
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever and dust or pet allergies can cause ongoing mucus.

commonCauses.title: Non-allergic rhinitis
commonCauses.detail: A long-term runny or blocked nose without an allergy.

commonCauses.title: Nasal polyps
commonCauses.detail: Soft growths that can cause long-term catarrh and reduced smell.

selfCare: Rinse your nose with salt water
Drink plenty of fluids and get enough rest
Keep the air moist and avoid very warm, dry rooms
Sleep with your head slightly raised
avoid: Things that trigger symptoms, such as smoke or known allergens
Dairy-free diets to clear mucus, which have no good evidence
Overusing decongestant sprays
seeDoctorIf: Catarrh lasts more than a few weeks
You develop new symptoms such as a sore throat, problems swallowing or loss of smell
It is affecting your sleep or daily life

name: Toothache
summary: Toothache is usually caused by tooth decay, a cracked tooth, gum problems or an infection. It needs a dentist to find and treat the cause.
redFlags: Swelling around the eye or in the neck
Swelling in the mouth or neck making it difficult to breathe, swallow or speak
Cannot open your mouth properly with spreading facial swelling and fever
urgentFlags: A swollen cheek or jaw
A high temperature with toothache
Pain when biting with red gums or a bad taste in the mouth
Severe pain that painkillers do not control

commonCauses.title: Tooth decay
commonCauses.detail: Cavities expose the sensitive inner part of the tooth.

commonCauses.title: Dental abscess
commonCauses.detail: A collection of pus from infection, causing throbbing pain and sometimes swelling.

commonCauses.title: Cracked tooth or damaged filling
commonCauses.detail: Pain often when biting or with hot and cold.

commonCauses.title: Gum disease or wisdom teeth
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed gums or an erupting wisdom tooth can cause pain.

commonCauses.title: Sinusitis
commonCauses.detail: Can cause aching in the upper back teeth.

selfCare: Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Use a pain-relieving mouth gel from a pharmacy
Rinse with warm salt water (adults only)
Eat soft foods and chew on the other side
Contact a dentist; if your dentist is closed, ask about emergency dental services
avoid: Holding aspirin against the gum, which can burn it
Very hot, cold or sugary food and drink
Using painkillers for weeks instead of getting the tooth treated
seeDoctorIf: Toothache lasts more than 2 days
Painkillers do not help
The tooth is sensitive or painful when you bite

name: Bleeding or swollen gums
summary: Gums that bleed when you brush are most often a sign of gum disease (gingivitis), which is common and can be reversed with good cleaning. A dentist can check and treat it.
redFlags: Bleeding that will not stop after 15 minutes of pressure
Very swollen gums with swelling spreading to the face or neck and difficulty swallowing or breathing
urgentFlags: Very sore and swollen gums
Teeth becoming loose or falling out
Bleeding gums with unexplained bruising, nosebleeds or feeling very tired
Painful, ulcerated gums with bad breath and fever

commonCauses.title: Gingivitis
commonCauses.detail: Plaque build-up along the gumline causing red, swollen gums that bleed.

commonCauses.title: Brushing too hard or flossing for the first time
commonCauses.detail: Can cause minor bleeding that settles.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Hormone changes make gums more likely to bleed.

commonCauses.title: Periodontitis
commonCauses.detail: More advanced gum disease that can loosen teeth.

commonCauses.title: Medicines or blood conditions
commonCauses.detail: Blood thinners or, rarely, blood disorders can cause bleeding gums.

selfCare: Brush twice a day for 2 minutes with a fluoride toothpaste and a soft brush
Clean between your teeth every day with floss or interdental brushes
Keep brushing gums that bleed; bleeding usually improves within 1 to 2 weeks
Stop smoking
Have regular dental check-ups and cleaning
avoid: Stopping brushing because your gums bleed
Brushing very hard with a hard brush
Sugary snacks and drinks between meals
seeDoctorIf: Your gums bleed when you brush or eat hard foods
Your gums are painful and swollen
You have bad breath that does not go away
You have not had a dental check-up for 2 years

name: Mouth ulcers
summary: Mouth ulcers are painful sores inside the mouth that are common and usually heal on their own within 1 to 2 weeks. An ulcer that lasts longer than 3 weeks should be checked.
redFlags: Mouth sores with a widespread rash, blistering skin or peeling, especially after a new medicine
Mouth swelling making it hard to breathe or swallow
urgentFlags: Unable to eat or drink because of pain, especially in a child
An ulcer that bleeds or becomes more painful, red and swollen
Many ulcers with a high temperature and feeling unwell

commonCauses.title: Minor injury
commonCauses.detail: Biting your cheek, sharp teeth, braces or dentures.

commonCauses.title: Stress, tiredness and hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Common triggers for recurring ulcers.

commonCauses.title: Certain foods or toothpastes
commonCauses.detail: Spicy or acidic foods, or toothpaste with sodium lauryl sulphate, can trigger ulcers.

commonCauses.title: Viral infections
commonCauses.detail: Such as hand, foot and mouth disease or cold sore virus.

commonCauses.title: Health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Low iron or vitamin B12, coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease can cause repeated ulcers.

selfCare: Use a soft toothbrush
Ask a pharmacist about pain-relieving gels, sprays or mouthwashes
Eat softer foods and drink cool drinks through a straw
Keep your mouth clean
avoid: Very spicy, salty, acidic or hard foods
Very hot drinks
Chewing gum
seeDoctorIf: An ulcer lasts longer than 3 weeks
An ulcer is different from ones you have had before, or near the back of the throat
You keep getting mouth ulcers
You also have ulcers elsewhere on the body, or painful, swollen joints

name: Dry mouth
summary: A dry mouth is rarely serious and is often caused by dehydration, medicines, mouth breathing or anxiety. Simple measures usually help.
redFlags: Dry mouth with confusion, drowsiness, fast breathing or not passing urine
Very dry mouth with extreme thirst, being sick and stomach pain in someone with diabetes
urgentFlags: Dry mouth with constant thirst, peeing a lot and weight loss
Dry mouth with signs of dehydration that are not improving with drinking

commonCauses.title: Dehydration
commonCauses.detail: Not drinking enough, sweating or being ill.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Many medicines list dry mouth as a side effect.

commonCauses.title: Mouth breathing
commonCauses.detail: A blocked nose or sleeping with your mouth open.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Stress can reduce saliva.

commonCauses.title: Health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Diabetes, Sjögren's syndrome and cancer treatment can cause a persistent dry mouth.

selfCare: Drink water regularly and take sips during meals
Chew sugar-free gum or suck sugar-free sweets
Ask a pharmacist about saliva substitutes, sprays or gels
Use a humidifier at night
Keep up good dental care, as a dry mouth raises the risk of decay
avoid: Alcohol, including alcohol-based mouthwash
Caffeine, smoking and sugary drinks
Salty or spicy food if it makes your mouth uncomfortable
seeDoctorIf: Your mouth is still dry after a few weeks of home or pharmacy treatment
It is making talking or eating difficult
You think a medicine is causing it
You also have dry eyes or need to pee a lot

name: Bad breath
summary: Bad breath is common and usually caused by bacteria in the mouth, especially when teeth, gums and tongue are not cleaned well. It can usually be treated at home.
redFlags: Fruity-smelling breath with vomiting, stomach pain, fast breathing or confusion, especially in someone with diabetes
urgentFlags: Bad breath with a painful swollen gum or face and a high temperature
Bad breath with a painful, ulcerated mouth and fever

commonCauses.title: Oral hygiene
commonCauses.detail: Food and bacteria build up on the teeth, gums and tongue.

commonCauses.title: Gum disease or tooth decay
commonCauses.detail: Infections in the mouth often cause a bad smell.

commonCauses.title: Strong foods, smoking and alcohol
commonCauses.detail: Garlic, onions, coffee, tobacco and alcohol affect breath.

commonCauses.title: Dry mouth
commonCauses.detail: Less saliva lets bacteria build up.

commonCauses.title: Other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Sinus or throat infections, acid reflux and some health conditions can cause bad breath.

selfCare: Brush teeth and gums twice a day for 2 minutes
Clean between your teeth daily and gently clean your tongue
Keep dentures clean and take them out at night
Drink water and chew sugar-free gum
Stop smoking
avoid: Relying on mouthwash or mints to hide the smell
Sugary snacks and drinks
Strong-smelling foods before social events if they affect you
seeDoctorIf: Bad breath does not go away after a few weeks of good cleaning
You have painful, bleeding or swollen gums
You have toothache or loose adult teeth
You have problems with your dentures

name: Sensitive teeth
summary: Sensitive teeth give a short, sharp pain with cold, hot, sweet or acidic foods. It is common and often caused by worn enamel or receding gums.
redFlags: Facial or neck swelling making it hard to breathe, swallow or open your mouth
urgentFlags: Pain that lingers for a long time or throbs on its own
Pain with a swollen gum or face, or a high temperature
A tooth that is cracked or broken

commonCauses.title: Worn enamel
commonCauses.detail: From brushing too hard, grinding or acidic food and drink.

commonCauses.title: Receding gums
commonCauses.detail: Expose the sensitive root surface of the tooth.

commonCauses.title: Tooth decay or a cracked tooth
commonCauses.detail: Can expose the inner tooth.

commonCauses.title: After dental treatment
commonCauses.detail: Fillings or whitening can cause short-term sensitivity.

selfCare: Use a toothpaste for sensitive teeth twice a day; it can take a few weeks to work
Brush gently with a soft toothbrush
Cut down on acidic foods and drinks, and use a straw for fizzy drinks
Wait about an hour after acidic food or drink before brushing
avoid: Brushing hard or side to side
Whitening toothpastes while teeth are sensitive
seeDoctorIf: Sensitivity has not improved after a few weeks of sensitive toothpaste
Sensitivity is in one tooth only
You grind your teeth

name: Swollen face or gum from a tooth (dental abscess)
summary: A dental abscess is a build-up of pus from an infection in a tooth or gum. It causes intense pain and swelling and will not go away on its own, so it needs urgent dental treatment.
redFlags: Finding it hard to breathe, speak or swallow
A swollen or painful eye, or sudden problems with eyesight
A lot of swelling in the mouth or neck
Finding it hard to open your mouth
Feeling very unwell with a high temperature, fast heartbeat or confusion
urgentFlags: You think you have a dental abscess
Intense toothache with a swollen face or jaw
A bad taste in the mouth with pain and swelling

commonCauses.title: Untreated tooth decay
commonCauses.detail: Bacteria reach the nerve and cause infection at the root.

commonCauses.title: Gum disease
commonCauses.detail: Infection can form a pocket of pus in the gum.

commonCauses.title: Cracked or damaged tooth
commonCauses.detail: Lets bacteria into the inner tooth.

selfCare: Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Eat soft foods and use a soft toothbrush
Avoid very hot or cold food and drink
Contact a dentist urgently, or emergency dental services if closed
avoid: Squeezing or bursting the swelling yourself
Waiting for it to go away; antibiotics alone do not cure an abscess
Using leftover antibiotics
seeDoctorIf: Any suspected abscess, even if the pain eases (the infection can remain)
Pain or swelling returns after treatment

name: Jaw pain or clicking jaw
summary: Jaw pain is often caused by a problem with the jaw joint and muscles (TMD), teeth grinding or a dental problem. It usually improves with self-care, but jaw pain with chest pain can be a sign of a heart attack.
redFlags: Jaw pain with chest pain, pressure or tightness
Jaw pain with shortness of breath, sweating or feeling sick and light-headed
Jaw locked open or closed after an injury, or a jaw that may be broken
Facial swelling making it hard to breathe or swallow
urgentFlags: Unable to eat or drink because of jaw pain
Jaw locking or difficulty opening the mouth fully
Jaw pain when chewing with headache, scalp tenderness or vision problems, especially if over 50

commonCauses.title: Temporomandibular disorder (TMD)
commonCauses.detail: Problems with the jaw joint and chewing muscles causing pain, clicking and stiffness.

commonCauses.title: Teeth grinding or clenching
commonCauses.detail: Often at night or with stress.

commonCauses.title: Dental problems
commonCauses.detail: Toothache, abscess or wisdom teeth can cause jaw pain.

commonCauses.title: Heart problems
commonCauses.detail: Angina or a heart attack can cause pain that spreads to the jaw.

commonCauses.title: Giant cell arteritis
commonCauses.detail: In older adults, jaw pain on chewing with headache needs urgent assessment.

selfCare: Eat soft foods and cut food into small pieces
Hold a warm or cold pack against the jaw
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Try relaxation to reduce clenching
Gently massage the jaw muscles
avoid: Chewing gum and hard or chewy foods
Opening your mouth very wide, for example big yawns
Resting your chin on your hand
seeDoctorIf: Jaw pain has not improved after 2 weeks
Pain is affecting eating or sleep
You have clicking with pain that keeps coming back
